title: Maximum Value after Insertion
statement:
The string `n` holds a (possibly huge) integer in decimal: an optional leading `'-'` for a negative number followed by digits, each from `1` to `9`. You also get a single digit `x` between `1` and `9`.

Insert exactly one copy of `x` somewhere among the digits of `n` (before the first digit, between two digits, or after the last one, but never in front of the `'-'` sign) so that the resulting number is as large as possible. Return that largest number as a string.
constraints: every digit of n is between 1 and 9
n is a valid integer: a negative n starts with '-'
notes:
## Intuition

All candidates have the same number of digits, so the comparison is decided at the first position where they differ. Trying every insertion point and comparing the results works, but costs O(n) per candidate and O(n²) overall.

For a positive number we want `x` to appear as early as possible, but only where it beats the digit it pushes right: put it before the first digit that is **smaller** than `x`. For a negative number the value is larger when the digits form a **smaller** magnitude, so put `x` before the first digit that is **larger** than `x`. If no such digit exists, `x` goes at the end.

## Approach

1. Turn `x` into the one-character string `digit` and note whether `n` is `negative`.
2. Start `i` just after the sign (index 1) for a negative number, otherwise at 0.
3. Move `i` right until a digit is larger than `digit` (negative case) or smaller than `digit` (positive case).
4. Return `n` with `digit` inserted at index `i` (the end, if the scan finished).

## Example 1, step by step

`n = "99"`, `x = 9`: `digit = "9"`, `negative = false`, `i = 0`. `"9" < "9"` is false, so `i` becomes 1; again false, so `i` becomes 2 and the loop ends. Inserting at the end gives `"999"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one scan plus building the result.
- Space: O(n) for the returned string.

## Pitfalls

- Do not stop at a digit equal to `x`: for `n = "56"` and `x = 5`, inserting before the first `5` gives `"556"`, but the scan correctly continues to give `"565"`. Both comparisons must be strict.
- Never insert before the `'-'`: start the scan at index 1 for negative numbers.
- `n` can be far longer than any numeric type, so work on the string, never convert it to a number.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `digit` | `x` as a one-character string |
| `negative` | whether `n` starts with `'-'` |
| `i` | the insertion index being tested |

narration.2: Work with x as a one-character string so it compares directly with the digits of n.
narration.3: Remember whether n is negative, because that flips which digits we want to pass.
narration.4: Start right after the minus sign for a negative number, since x cannot go before it.
narration.6: Scan the digits until we find where x should go.
narration.7: For a negative number, a digit bigger than x is where x makes the magnitude smaller...
narration.10: For a positive number, a digit smaller than x is where x makes the value bigger...
narration.13: This digit should stay ahead of x; move on to the next position.
narration.15: Insert x at the chosen index, or at the end if the scan never stopped.
